listing_view.reasoning: Subscription went from ~0.6x on day two to 12.15x on the final day, with nearly all demand arriving in the last hours — typical of QIB-led institutional interest and a strong listing signal. At 12.8x latest EPS (139/10.82), pricing is not aggressive by Indian mainboard standards. The absence of GMP and anchor data is a gap, but the late demand surge alone supports an above-average debut.

longterm_view.reasoning: PAT is essentially flat (~3% CAGR over two years) while borrowings exploded from ~₹1,319mn to ~₹16,826mn — leverage rose roughly 10x to produce almost no incremental profit, and even the document's own printed debt-to-equity doesn't reconcile with ours (0.39 vs 0.546). Cash conversion is weak (OCF/PAT ~0.44; ~0.31 vs EBITDA), meaning a large share of reported profit never arrived as cash. For an ARC, where earnings are only as good as recoveries actually collected, that combination is a genuine orange flag.

governance.reasoning: Promoter shares are partially pledged in all three years shown [promoters, page 273], [promoters, page 332], and the litigation extracts show the company reporting no criminal cases against it [litigation, page 434] — the SBI cheque-dishonour cases appear to be by SBI, not against the issuer. Pledging keeps this below neutral; nothing rises to a red flag.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Borrowings grew ~12x in three years while PAT grew ~3%, so each rupee of new leverage is earning little; the document itself flags refinancing-cost risk [business, page 200].

key_risks.risk: Poor cash conversion of reported profit
key_risks.why_it_matters: Only ~31-44% of reported profit showed up as operating cash, and in an asset-reconstruction business cash recovery is the business model; the prospectus admits cash flows may be adversely affected [business, page 204].
Promoters have partially pledged shares in each of the last three years, creating potential forced-sale pressure and signalling tight promoter finances [promoters, page 273].
Our computation (0.546) does not match the figure printed in the document (0.39); unexplained balance-sheet mismatches in a filing are a disclosure-quality concern.

answers.question: check receivables and inventory against the sales growth
answers.answer: Not answerable — no receivables, inventory, or debtor-days figures were provided. What I can say: revenue grew only modestly (₹5,964mn to ₹7,530mn on the business page series, ~26% over two years) while borrowings grew ~12x, so whatever drove the balance-sheet expansion, it was not sales growth. Receivables data would be needed to say whether the top line is cash-backed.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: Receivables/ageing data and security-receipt cash-flow detail showing recoveries actually collected would resolve the cash-conversion worry; a clear fresh-issue vs OFS split and ROE/ROCE disclosure would tell me whether the leverage is funding accretive acquisitions or papering over weak returns.
